A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ProCAD study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset evaluations, coding-agent experiments, and simulated clarification experiments in Sections 6.1–6.3 and Tables 1–5, with additional analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds human-interaction experiments, human validation of automatic judging, failure analysis, and interaction-policy ablations.

M1.justification: The two Qwen2.5-7B agents, data-construction pipeline, SFT objectives, and accept-or-batch-clarify procedure remain unchanged. Appendix K evaluates alternative interaction policies without changing the proposed ProCAD procedure.

E1.justification: Section 6.4 extends evaluation from LLM-simulated interaction to human-authored ambiguous prompts and human answers, using 100 examples from the existing CAD dataset. This introduces a substantively different interaction environment, while retaining the underlying geometry domain and original datasets.

E2.justification: Appendix K adds Claude Sonnet 4.5 variants using one-question-per-round, forced-follow-up, and single-question policies, evaluated alongside ProCAD and the existing all-at-once approach. The original model baseline sets remain unchanged; the human evaluation reuses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GPT-4o-mini, and Claude Sonnet 4.5.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include CAD-expert scoring of human interactions, a separate 100-example comparison of human and LLM judgments, and controlled policy experiments holding the clarifier and coder fixed. Appendix K introduces measured end-to-end latency and per-round ambiguity resolution. Existing training budgets, splits, and benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained qualitative examples, v2 adds systematic analysis of ProCAD's failures in Appendix J, controlled interaction-policy and round-level ablations in Appendix K, and human validation of automatic scoring in Section 6.4. These directly examine remaining errors, evaluation reliability, and the justification for batching clarification questions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed/run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new human-agreement and failure percentages add point results, without introducing uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Existing result tables retain their numerical values. New Table 6 reports mean CD multiplied by 10^3 of 1.28 for ProCAD versus 9.72 for Claude Sonnet 4.5 under the same human-evaluation setting and fixed ProCAD-coder; both have 12.2% invalidity. Tables 11–12 add policy-quality, latency, and round-level results. Appendix J adds failure statistics, and Section 6.4 reports over 96% human–LLM judgment agreement.

T1.justification: The MDP formulation, action space, reward, SFT objectives, and assumptions supporting the two-round policy remain unchanged. The added policy experiments provide empirical evidence rather than new mathematical derivations, assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about proactive clarification, curated supervision, sample-efficient fine-tuning, and improved CAD generation. The new evaluations support these claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: v2 newly identifies missed simultaneous ambiguities and occasional incorrect incorporation of answers as ProCAD limitations. It interprets policy experiments as showing harmful under-clarification and diminishing returns from forced extra rounds, and adds arguments about human transfer and judge reliability. Section 3 also removes the speculative claim that decomposition mitigates reward hacking.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code and datasets from a promised future release to reported public availability. This is an access-status disclosure, although availability cannot be independently verified from the PDFs. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, training times, and full system prompts are retained; the prompt appendix changes from J to L.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds Zhao et al. (2021a, 2021b, 2024), while Amodei et al. (2016) is removed with the reward-hacking discussion. The broader positioning remains intact. PR-CAD's updated authorship and date refer to the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. Changes include localized wording corrections, Section 6.4, new Appendices J–K, updated appendix navigation, and acknowledgments and impact statements. These are targeted insertions and edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, with changed typography, running headers, and widespread resizing and repositioning of displays. It adds Tables 6, 11, and 12. The four existing figures retain their substantive content, while the original appendix tables are renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central interaction claims. Section 6.4 addresses v1's reliance on simulated users through human-authored prompts, human answers, expert ratings, and validation of LLM judging. Appendices J–K expose ProCAD's own failure conditions and test the quality–latency rationale for its interaction policy. The human study remains limited to 100 source examples, and uncertainty and annotator reporting remain sparse, but the added validation and critical analysis materially improve the paper's credibility.
